paragraphs.text: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan said he spends roughly $100,000 to $200,000 a year on AI tokens, the units that AI companies use to bill for model usage. He gave the estimate on an episode of The Builders, the podcast hosted by Walter Isaacson, which was set to be released on November 3, 2026, according to TechCrunch. Tan described the figure as a rough estimate.

Tan has joked in the past about suffering from "cyber psychosis" and has said he sometimes barely sleeps because he is excited to work with his agents, TechCrunch reported. On the podcast he said he uses agents for a long list of work projects and coding tasks, and that he wants to help other people understand what agents can do.
Agents that read his email and notes

According to TechCrunch, Tan said his personal agent has access to his email, his Dropbox and his Apple Notes, as well as therapy notes he has kept for about 20 years. He described agents as able to help with almost anything in daily life and compared them to a Jiminy Cricket on his shoulder. NewsBytes also reported his use of agents to sort email and retrieve personal notes written two decades ago.

Tan said he used an agent to research Isaacson's podcast before the interview and to prepare for likely questions. Superpower Daily noted that his argument rests on an assistant that already holds personal context and can anticipate what he needs.
He has also published a set of 23 Claude Code skills on GitHub under the name gstack, which he presents as a way to show others what agents can do, according to TechCrunch and NewsBytes.

Inside Y Combinator, Tan said, an internal agent called Stray Light acts as a company brain. He said it has a personality and holds context on every founder the accelerator has backed, every person who has emailed Y Combinator and every application it has received. He told Isaacson that the firm is rebuilding the way it operates around these tools.

Tan was an early adopter of OpenClaw and now calls himself a power user, TechCrunch reported. He advised against treating agents like traditional software and criticized people who focus so much on repeatability and safety that they lose what makes agents useful.

Tan said he expects personal AI agents to become mainstream once costs fall, but called them too expensive right now. He acknowledged that his own spending is a privilege that most people do not have. He also argued that free agents run by large technology companies may not be the answer, pointing to Meta's control over its feed algorithm, and said he favors a personal AI that users control and program themselves.

Tan's numbers are his own estimate and have not been independently checked, but they show how far heavy agent use has moved beyond a monthly chatbot subscription. A budget in the six figures is out of reach for nearly every consumer, which supports his point that personal agents depend on lower prices before they can spread widely. His description of an agent reading years of private notes also shows how much access these tools need to be useful, a tradeoff many users may weigh differently than he does.

Watch whether the full episode of The Builders adds detail on which models and services make up Tan's token bill, and whether Y Combinator shares more about Stray Light or opens any of its tools to the startups it funds.
